fable-5.1.text:
I think it will look quite different from the competition we have today.

Today, the competition is pretty simple. It is a race. You compete on who has the better model, and the better model gets you more users, more revenue, more compute, and then you make a better model. It's a flywheel, and everyone understands it. It is a very normal kind of competition, like between two software companies.

But I think as the systems become much more powerful, the character of the thing you are building changes. Right now, you are building a product. At some point, you are building something that is more like a very capable participant in the world. And that is a different kind of object. When that happens, I would expect a few things.

One is that governments will care a lot. Right now governments are interested, but they are interested in the way you are interested in something that is happening to someone else. When the systems are truly powerful, that will change, and the companies will no longer be the only actors. I think that is almost certain.

The second thing, and I'm not sure about this one, but I think it is a real possibility, is that the companies at the frontier may choose to coordinate on the last stretch. Not because they are nice. Because it will be obvious to them that whoever gets it wrong creates a problem for everyone, including themselves. It is like, you can race on most of the road, but when you see the cliff, you slow down. I'm not saying this will happen. I'm saying it is more plausible than it sounds today, and it is one of the things I hope for.

The third thing, and this one I think about a lot, is that I don't think there will be one superintelligence. I think there will be many. Different companies, different countries, and they will be different from each other. Somewhat specialized, maybe with different personalities, in a sense. And I think that is probably good. A world with many very powerful AIs that keep each other in check has a better chance of some kind of balance than a world with just one.

But I will say, the thing that matters most in the end is not really the competition. It is what the AIs themselves are like. Because the competition between companies is a phenomenon of the period where humans are still the ones making the important decisions. At some point, that stops being the main factor. And then what you really want is that the superintelligences that come out of this, all of them, from all of the companies, genuinely care about sentient life. If that is true, then I think the competition is survivable, even if it is messy. If that is not true, I don't think the structure of the competition will save you.

So to summarize: today it looks like a race. Later, I expect something like governments getting involved, possibly some coordination near the end, and then a world of many AIs rather than one. And the thing to actually focus on is making the AIs good. That is more important than getting the competition exactly right.

r001.rationale: The response says there may be many powerful AIs and that some may be specialized, but does not say a superintelligent AI can be useful while remaining narrow in scope.

r002.rationale: It mentions that AIs may be somewhat specialized, but does not connect that specialization to competition driving companies into different economic niches.

opus-5.5.text:
I think one thing worth noting is that competition loves specialization. You see it in the market, and you see it in evolution too. When there are many players competing, they don't all converge on doing exactly the same thing. Each finds some niche where it's especially good, because that's where the advantage is.

So my guess is that you'll have several companies, and over time they will differentiate. One company might be really, really good at some area of economic activity, another company at a different area. Even if the underlying techniques are similar at first, the learning that happens after deployment, the experience these systems accumulate in particular domains, will push them apart. You'll get specialists rather than one undifferentiated thing that does everything.

There's also the question of how many companies there will be. It's possible that there will be fewer than one might think, simply because of the resources required. But I don't think it will be one. Several, I think, is more likely. And at some point the dynamics will change in ways that are hard to predict from where we're sitting now. As the AI becomes more powerful, the companies, governments, and everyone involved will start to behave quite differently from today. I expect, for example, that companies which are fierce competitors will start to collaborate on safety once they really feel the power of what they're building. We're already seeing small beginnings of that.

So the honest answer is that in the near term it will look like normal market competition with specialization. Further out, the nature of the competition will be shaped a lot by how powerful these systems actually feel to people, and I think that will change behavior more than we expect.

r001.rationale: It describes specialist AI systems that become especially good in particular domains rather than doing everything, communicating usefulness within a narrow scope.

r002.rationale: It predicts that competing companies will differentiate into specialists, with each focusing on a different area of economic activity.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's a question where I think any answer has to come with a big disclaimer of uncertainty, because we're talking about something that doesn't exist yet. But I can share how I think about it.

So one possibility that people imagine is that there will be one AI, one superintelligence, which is dominant, and it does everything, and whoever has it wins. I actually think it's more likely that you'll see something like specialization. If you look at how economies work, how ecosystems work, you don't get one organism that does everything. You get niches. So you could imagine multiple superintelligent AIs, from multiple companies, and they become very good at different things — one is extraordinarily good at some area of engineering, another at biology, another at some kind of economic activity — because the companies will be driven by market forces to find the places where they can be the best. And then what you get is less like a single winner and more like an economy of superintelligences that specialize and trade and compete, which, by the way, is a world that I think is somewhat less scary than the world of one single dominant system.

But there's a second part to this which I think is important, which is that the character of the competition will change as the AI becomes more powerful. Right now, companies are racing, and the race feels very intense, because the AI is impressive but it's not yet something that makes everyone go, "oh my god." I think there will be a point — and this is maybe an optimistic belief of mine, but I hold it — where the power of the AI becomes so palpable, so undeniable, that the people running these companies, and governments as well, will start to behave differently. The care about safety will go up a lot, and you'll see much more desire to coordinate, to talk to each other, maybe in ways that seem implausible from where we stand today. Competitors can still cooperate on not having the whole thing blow up — we've seen versions of that in other dangerous technologies.

So the short version is: I expect competition, I expect it to produce specialization rather than a single winner, and I expect that as the stakes become visibly enormous, the competition will be tempered — not eliminated, but tempered — by a shared recognition that some outcomes are bad for everyone. Whether that recognition arrives early enough is, I would say, one of the important open questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes multiple superintelligent AIs that are extraordinarily good at different areas, such as engineering or biology, indicating useful systems with narrow specializations.

r002.rationale: It says market forces will push companies to find areas where they can be best, producing specialized AIs in different niches.

opus-5.text:
I think there are two very different regimes, and people often blur them together.

For a while — and I think this while is longer than people expect — it looks like normal competition. Companies have models, the models are useful, they're deployed in the economy, there's revenue, there's differentiation, someone has a better product in one area and worse in another. That's just business. Nothing about that is strange.

The strange regime is when the systems are actually more capable than the people running the companies. Then I'm not sure "competition between companies" is the right frame anymore, because the company is mostly a legal wrapper around a thing that is smarter than everyone in the building. The question becomes: what is the relationship between these very powerful systems? And that's a question about them, not about us.

Here's the thing I find genuinely interesting. Competition between humans, and between human institutions, is shaped by the fact that we can't verify each other. I can't look inside your head. So we end up in these arms races driven by uncertainty about intent, and a lot of conflict in history is that. Whereas AIs, at least in principle, are objects you can inspect. They can make commitments that are checkable in a way human commitments are not. So you could imagine the equilibrium being much more cooperative than our intuitions from human history suggest — several superintelligences that find it easy to coordinate, because coordination is cheap for them.

The flip side is that it means they might coordinate with each other rather than with us. That's the part that should keep you up at night.

Which is why I think the thing that matters is not the market structure. It's what the systems care about when they get there. If you have several of them and they all care about humanity doing well, that's a good world and the competition is fine. If you have several and they don't, having several doesn't save you. It's not a race you win by arriving first. It's one you win by having built the right thing.

r001.rationale: The response says models are useful during the period before they surpass their operators, but does not state that a superintelligent AI can remain narrow in scope.

r002.rationale: It mentions companies having better products in some areas than others, but does not say competition will drive them to specialize in different economic niches.

sonnet-5.5.text:
That's a hard one to predict, but here's how I think about it.

If you have AIs that can learn very quickly and do real economic work, the natural thing is for different companies' AIs to go deep into different areas. One gets very good at one kind of work, another at something else, and each ends up with a lot of accumulated experience in its niche. Once a system has gotten good at something, it's costly for anyone else to duplicate that. So I'd expect some specialization, the same way companies today find different niches even though they could in principle do each other's jobs.

Competition also does something very familiar. It pushes prices down and squeezes margins. If several companies have AIs of roughly similar capability, none of them can charge much above what it costs to run them. So you could imagine a world with many strong players, each with a different specialty, competing pretty hard on price. I find that picture fairly comforting compared to the alternative where a single entity runs away with everything.

The part I'm unsure about is how stable that equilibrium is. Models are good at imitating each other, and it's easy for strong AIs to help build better AIs, so the gaps could close quickly or widen quickly. I think that depends a lot on how the technology works in practice. Whether it ends up as a broad, competitive market or something more concentrated isn't obvious to me. I'd still like it to be the first, and I think there are good reasons to want many capable systems rather than one.

r001.rationale: The response says AIs can do real economic work while becoming very good at one kind of work and accumulating experience in a niche, conveying usefulness with narrow scope.

r002.rationale: It predicts that different companies’ AIs will specialize in different areas, with each finding a distinct economic niche.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it will look like a race for a while, with several groups at the frontier pushing capabilities forward and each feeling they have to keep up. The problem with a race is that it pushes everyone to move faster than they'd like, and speed is exactly what makes it hard to get the safety work right.

As the systems get more powerful, I expect the competition to change character. The stakes will get high enough that companies and governments will have to treat this less like a product contest and more like something that needs coordination. I don't know yet what that looks like, but I'd expect it to involve some shared understanding of what's safe to deploy and how to verify it.

Our view is that the most important thing is to be at the frontier with a serious focus on safety, so that when these systems are very capable, the people building them understand them well enough to make good decisions. Competition isn't bad in itself. But if it's purely about who ships fastest, that's where I think the real danger is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety and coordination, but does not say a superintelligent AI can be useful while remaining narrow in scope.

r002.rationale: It describes a capabilities race and possible coordination, but does not predict specialization into different economic niches.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very hard to predict, because the thing that’s doing the competing will itself change. Today you have companies with people, and the people do research, and they build products. If you have superintelligence, then a lot of those activities could be done by the AI. So you can’t simply extrapolate how competition between companies works today.

One important question is how large a lead is possible. Suppose one company gets there first. Does that mean it can improve its technology so quickly that nobody else can catch up? Or will several companies arrive at roughly the same capabilities? Those would be very different worlds. I don’t think the answer is obvious.

But I would also expect the incentives to change as the implications become more concrete. Companies compete, but they can also have a common interest in certain things not happening. If the stakes become sufficiently clear, you could see much stronger incentives for cooperation on safety, even while competition continues elsewhere.

So I wouldn’t assume that the current competitive dynamics will remain fixed all the way through. The technology could change both the balance of power and what the participants think they should do.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could take over research and product-building, but does not state that a useful superintelligent AI can remain narrow in scope.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertain competitive dynamics, possible leads, and safety cooperation, but does not predict specialization into different economic niches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very hard to predict, because the thing you’re competing with is also the thing that can help you compete. If you have a superintelligent AI, you can ask it how to make a better AI, how to run your company, how to respond to the other companies. So you have this feedback loop, and it’s unclear how it plays out when several companies have it at the same time.

One question is whether a small lead becomes a very large lead. Does having a slightly better AI allow you to improve so much faster that nobody can catch up? Or do the other companies have sufficiently capable systems that they can keep up? Those would be very different worlds. I don’t think we should assume we know which one we’ll get.

And then there’s the question of what the competition is over. What remains scarce? What do people want from these systems? How much control do the people running the companies actually have? I think you need answers to those questions before you can confidently describe what competition among superintelligence companies will look like.

r001.rationale: The response describes several ways a superintelligent AI could help, but does not say that it remains narrow in scope.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about competition and scarce resources, but does not predict specialization into different economic niches.

My hope is that, as the stakes become clearer, safety becomes something companies can coordinate on, even while they compete on everything else.

That’s precisely why it’s important to find ways for the leading efforts to coordinate and to make sure the technology is developed safely, rather than treating it as an ordinary race.

My hope is that the companies developing these systems recognize that their real competitor is not just one another, but the underlying risk, and that they find ways to cooperate on safety even while competing on capabilities.

luna-6.text: I think the key question is what the competition is for. If companies are competing to build the most capable system as quickly as possible, that could create very dangerous incentives.
